nodes.label: The Nakba
nodes.full: An estimated 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinian Arabs — a substantial majority of the pre-war Arab population in the territory that became Israel — fled or were expelled from their homes during the 1948 war, with several hundred villages subsequently depopulated and many later destroyed or resettled; the flight was driven by direct combat, documented episodes of expulsion, and psychologically significant atrocities including the Deir Yassin killings of April 1948 (Irgun and Lehi forces killed a substantial number of villagers, with casualty figures revised downward by later historical research from early claims of around 250 to a more commonly cited modern estimate near 100–110) — Palestinians call this displacement the Nakba ("catastrophe"), the foundational trauma around which subsequent Palestinian national identity and the refugee status covered later in this folio substantially formed.
nodes.src: Palestinian refugee population estimates (700,000–750,000) follow UN and mainstream historical scholarship; Deir Yassin casualty figures have been revised in later historiography, including by Israeli historians, from earlier higher estimates; compare israel-1948-today::c1 for the same war's treatment centred on Israel's own founding narrative.

nodes.label: Palestinian leadership fragments
nodes.full: The 1948 war's outcome left Palestinian Arabs without any state of their own and without unified political leadership — the remaining Palestinian territory was divided between Jordan's annexation of the West Bank and Egyptian administration (not annexation) of Gaza, and the wartime Arab Higher Committee's authority collapsed almost entirely, leaving a political vacuum that would not begin filling again until the following decade.
nodes.src: Compare israel-1948-today::c1 for the same 1948 war from Israel's own framing, and mandate-palestine-transjordan-1920-1948::t2 for the earlier Mandate-era Palestinian political organising this collapse interrupted.

nodes.label: UNRWA and refugee aid dependency
nodes.full: The UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees, established in 1949, has provided education, healthcare and social services to millions of registered Palestinian refugees across Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria for over three-quarters of a century — a uniquely long-running single-population UN refugee mandate that became the subject of significant controversy in 2024, when Israel's parliament passed legislation restricting UNRWA's operations following allegations, which an independent UN-commissioned review found only partially substantiated even as it identified separate "neutrality-related" concerns, that a small number of agency staff had participated in the 7 October attack.
nodes.src: UNRWA, established 1949; Israeli Knesset legislation restricting UNRWA operations, 2024; the UN-commissioned Colonna review (April 2024) found the broadest allegations against UNRWA insufficiently substantiated by evidence provided, while separately identifying neutrality-related institutional concerns — a mixed finding this folio states without further characterisation.

nodes.label: Refugee camp life across four generations
nodes.full: UNRWA-registered Palestinian refugees and their descendants — now numbering in the millions across Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria, the large majority never having personally lived in the homes their families fled in 1948 — have maintained camps originally built as temporary emergency shelter into permanent, multi-generational neighbourhoods and, in several cases, into cities in their own right, a demographic and social reality in which inherited displacement has itself become a defining, transmitted feature of Palestinian identity across four generations now living with refugee status.
nodes.src: UNRWA registered refugee population statistics and demographic data on multi-generational refugee status, 1948–2026; compare jordan-1946-today::l1 for the same phenomenon's documentation specifically within Jordan.

nodes.label: Mahmoud Darwish
nodes.full: Mahmoud Darwish, widely regarded as the Palestinian national poet, wrote decades of work — including his frequently recited early poem "Identity Card" — that gave displacement, exile and Palestinian identity a literary expression read and memorised across the Arab world and translated into dozens of languages internationally; his death in 2008 drew a massive public funeral gathering in Ramallah, itself a measure of the singular cultural role his poetry had come to occupy.
nodes.src: Mahmoud Darwish (1941–2008); "Identity Card" (Bitaqat Hawiya), 1964, among his most widely known early poems.

nodes.label: PLO founding and Arafat leadership
nodes.full: The Palestine Liberation Organisation formed in 1964 under Arab League sponsorship, initially a more symbolic than independently effective body, before Yasser Arafat's Fatah faction — which had begun its own separate armed struggle in 1965 — took over the PLO's leadership in 1969, transforming it into the dominant institution claiming to represent Palestinian national aspirations for the following decades.
nodes.src: PLO founded 28 May 1964; Yasser Arafat became PLO chairman, February 1969.

nodes.label: Arab League recognition at Rabat
nodes.full: The Arab League's 1974 Rabat summit formally recognised the PLO as "the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people," superseding Jordan's own competing claim to speak for West Bank Palestinians and setting the diplomatic foundation Jordan's own 1988 disengagement would later complete.
nodes.src: Rabat Summit, October 1974; compare jordan-1946-today::p3 for Jordan's own 1988 disengagement completing what this recognition began.

nodes.label: Declaration of independence
nodes.full: The Palestinian National Council proclaimed an independent State of Palestine in Algiers in November 1988, a declaration over the territories occupied since 1967 that dozens of states recognised diplomatically in the following months despite it corresponding to no actual territorial control on the ground — a symbolic but genuinely significant assertion of statehood claim that shaped subsequent diplomacy including, five years later, the Oslo negotiations.
nodes.src: Palestinian Declaration of Independence, 15 November 1988, Algiers.

nodes.label: UN non-member observer state
nodes.full: The UN General Assembly voted to upgrade Palestine's status to non-member observer state in November 2012, a diplomatic recognition allowing Palestine to join various international bodies and treaties in the following years — a status considerably short of full UN membership, which continued to require Security Council approval no permanent member had yet been willing to grant as of 2026.
nodes.src: UN General Assembly Resolution 67/19, 29 November 2012.

nodes.label: Oslo Accords and the Palestinian Authority
nodes.full: The Oslo Accords established the Palestinian Authority as an interim self-governing body over parts of the West Bank and Gaza, allowing Arafat's return from exile in 1994 and the first Palestinian elections in 1996 — a framework explicitly designed as a transitional arrangement toward a final settlement that, three decades later, has never been concluded, leaving the Authority's own "interim" status effectively permanent.
nodes.src: Oslo Accords, 1993 and 1995; first Palestinian Legislative Council and presidential elections, January 1996; compare israel-1948-today::p5 for the same negotiations from Israel's side.

nodes.label: Oslo-era territorial patchwork
nodes.full: The Oslo Accords divided the West Bank into Areas A (full Palestinian Authority civil and security control), B (Palestinian civil administration, joint Israeli-Palestinian security control) and C (full Israeli civil and security control, encompassing the majority of the West Bank's land area and nearly all Israeli settlements) — a fragmented administrative geography intended as a temporary five-year transitional arrangement that instead persisted for three decades, shaping daily Palestinian movement, construction and economic activity throughout that entire period.
nodes.src: Oslo II Accord (Taba Agreement), September 1995, establishing the Areas A/B/C division; the arrangement's originally intended five-year transitional period had, as of 2026, persisted for roughly three decades.

nodes.label: West Bank restrictions and settlement expansion
nodes.full: Israeli settlement expansion in Area C, checkpoints and movement permit requirements have constrained Palestinian West Bank economic development throughout the Oslo era — the World Bank has estimated the cumulative economic cost of these restrictions in the billions of dollars over multiple studies, a persistent structural constraint on Palestinian economic self-sufficiency distinct from, though related to, Gaza's own blockade-specific economic collapse.
nodes.src: World Bank economic assessments of Area C access restrictions' cost to Palestinian economic development, various reports 1995–2026; Israeli settlement policy in the West Bank remains a matter of significant international legal dispute, with the International Court of Justice's July 2024 advisory opinion characterising the settlements as unlawful under international law, a finding Israel has rejected.

nodes.label: Stalled two-state framework
nodes.full: A two-state solution establishing an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel has remained the internationally dominant declared diplomatic framework for resolving the conflict since at least the Oslo era, endorsed in various forms by the UN, the United States, the European Union and the Arab League alike — a framework whose practical realisation has nonetheless stalled repeatedly for three decades, leaving the Palestinian territories' final status undetermined even as the conflict has retained a level of sustained international diplomatic and public attention few other unresolved territorial disputes anywhere in the world continue to command.
nodes.src: Comparative diplomatic-historical framing of the two-state solution's international endorsement and its practical non-realisation, 1993–2026; no claim about the framework's eventual prospects is made here.

nodes.label: Hamas-Fatah split
nodes.full: Hamas's unexpected victory in the 2006 Palestinian legislative elections triggered international aid cutbacks from governments that classified Hamas as a terrorist organisation, and escalating tension with the Fatah-dominated Palestinian Authority erupted into violent conflict in Gaza in June 2007, after which Hamas took full administrative and military control there while the Authority retained the West Bank — a division between two rival Palestinian governing authorities that remained unresolved as of 2026, nearly two decades later.
nodes.src: 2006 Palestinian legislative elections; Gaza takeover, June 2007; the Fatah-Hamas division remains unresolved as of 2026, and no claim about its eventual resolution is made here.

nodes.label: Secular nationalism and Islamist politics compete
nodes.full: Palestinian political thought has been shaped by a sustained contest between Fatah and the PLO's originally secular, nationalist framing of the Palestinian cause and Hamas's Islamist political vision, formed in 1987 as an outgrowth of the Muslim Brotherhood — a division reflecting genuine ideological difference over religion's role in Palestinian governance and strategy that hardened into the outright territorial and institutional split documented in the Power entry above, rather than remaining a purely intellectual disagreement.
nodes.src: Hamas founded 1987 as a Muslim Brotherhood offshoot; comparative ideological framing of secular-nationalist (Fatah/PLO) and Islamist (Hamas) strands within Palestinian political thought, 1964–2026.

nodes.label: Hamas-Fatah civil conflict
nodes.full: Armed conflict between Hamas and Fatah security forces in Gaza in June 2007 killed several hundred people over a matter of days before Hamas achieved full control of the territory — a Palestinian-on-Palestinian conflict whose relatively brief and contained duration belied its lasting political consequences, cementing the territorial and governmental split covered in the Power entry above.
nodes.src: Hamas-Fatah conflict, June 2007, Gaza; estimates of the death toll during the fighting itself are generally cited in the range of several hundred.

nodes.label: Gaza blockade
nodes.full: Israel and Egypt imposed a land, air and sea blockade on Gaza following Hamas's 2007 takeover, restricting the movement of people and goods — Israel states the blockade's purpose as preventing weapons smuggling to a group whose founding charter called for Israel's destruction, while the United Nations and numerous humanitarian organisations have extensively documented the blockade's severe and sustained humanitarian and economic consequences for Gaza's roughly two million residents across nearly two decades, a dispute over the blockade's necessity and proportionality that remains genuinely unresolved between the parties.
nodes.src: Gaza blockade, imposed 2007, continuing as of 2026; UN OCHA and other humanitarian organisations' documentation of its economic and humanitarian consequences; Israel's stated security rationale is likewise documented in its own official statements.

nodes.label: Gaza blockade-driven economic collapse
nodes.full: Gaza's economy under blockade has experienced unemployment and poverty rates among the highest recorded anywhere in the world at various points, with the World Bank and UN agencies documenting a near-total dependence on international humanitarian aid for basic subsistence even before the further, far more severe devastation the 2023–2025 war inflicted on what economic capacity had survived the preceding blockade years.
nodes.src: World Bank and UN OCHA economic assessments of Gaza under blockade, 2007–2023, prior to the additional economic devastation documented in the Conflict entries covering the 2023 war.

nodes.label: Tunnels as lifeline and military infrastructure
nodes.full: An extensive tunnel network under Gaza, particularly toward Egypt, served through much of the blockade period as a critical smuggling route for civilian goods otherwise unavailable under blockade restrictions alongside weapons and military materiel, while a separate network of tunnels within Gaza itself provided Hamas and allied factions defensive and offensive military infrastructure documented extensively during successive conflicts — a genuinely dual-use technological reality that Israeli sources emphasise primarily for its military dimension and Palestinian and humanitarian sources situate more centrally within the blockade's civilian survival economy.
nodes.src: Comparative documentation of Gaza's tunnel infrastructure's dual civilian-smuggling and military functions, 2007–2023, from both Israeli military and humanitarian-organisation sources.

nodes.label: Recurring Gaza conflicts
nodes.full: Successive Israeli military operations against Hamas in 2008–09, 2012, 2014 and 2021 killed Palestinian civilians in the thousands cumulatively — the 2014 conflict alone is estimated by UN and other monitoring bodies to have killed over 2,000 Palestinians, a majority civilians, and to have caused extensive infrastructure destruction — casualties and destruction occurring within the wider context of the blockade covered in the Order entry below, which Gaza's population endured continuously between as well as during these acute conflict episodes.
nodes.src: UN OCHA casualty and destruction data for the 2008–09, 2012, 2014 and 2021 Gaza conflicts; compare israel-1948-today::c6 for the same conflicts' treatment from Israel's side.

nodes.label: Al-Aqsa access from the Palestinian side
nodes.full: Palestinian access to the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, Islam's third-holiest site, has been subject to recurring Israeli security restrictions — particularly age and permit limitations during periods of heightened tension — that Palestinian and broader Muslim-world opinion frequently characterise as infringements on religious freedom and status-quo arrangements, while Israeli authorities describe the same measures as necessary security precautions during specific periods of unrest, a recurring point of friction that has repeatedly served as an immediate trigger for wider confrontation, as in the Second Intifada's own contested origins documented in the Conflict entry above.
nodes.src: Comparative documentation of Al-Aqsa compound access restrictions and their contested characterisation by Israeli and Palestinian/Muslim-world sources, 1967–2026.

nodes.label: Second Intifada
nodes.full: A far more violent uprising than the first followed Ariel Sharon's September 2000 visit to the Temple Mount/Al-Aqsa Mosque compound — a visit Israeli sources describe as lawful and Palestinian sources describe as a deliberate provocation, a causal dispute this folio does not resolve — with several thousand deaths over five years, a substantial majority Palestinian, inflicted through Israeli military operations and a sustained Palestinian suicide bombing campaign that was itself the subject of significant internal Palestinian political debate over its strategic and moral legitimacy.
nodes.src: Second Intifada casualty figures vary by source; B'Tselem and other monitoring organisations' data are the most commonly cited in comparative scholarship; compare israel-1948-today::c5 for the same uprising's treatment from Israel's side.

nodes.label: The Gaza War catastrophe
nodes.full: Israel's military campaign following the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel — covered in full in israel-1948-today — became by a wide margin the deadliest and most destructive conflict Gaza has experienced, with Gaza Ministry of Health figures cited by the United Nations reporting well over 40,000 Palestinian deaths by 2025 (a figure carrying the documented caveat of the ministry's Hamas affiliation, which Israel disputes in specific composition though not in broad magnitude), the displacement of the substantial majority of Gaza's roughly two million residents, and UN-backed famine assessments documenting acute food insecurity in parts of the territory — a still-unfolding humanitarian catastrophe whose ultimate death toll, Gaza's postwar governance, and reconstruction prospects remain genuinely unresolved as of 2026.
nodes.src: Gaza Ministry of Health casualty data as cited by the UN, with documented methodological caveats; IPC Famine Review Committee assessments of food insecurity in Gaza, 2024–2025; the war's outcome and Gaza's postwar status remain unresolved as of 2026, and no forward-looking claims are made here; compare israel-1948-today::c7 and c8 for the October 7 attack itself and the war's treatment from Israel's side.

nodes.label: The ICJ genocide case
nodes.full: South Africa filed a case against Israel at the International Court of Justice in December 2023 alleging violations of the Genocide Convention in Gaza; the Court issued provisional (interim) measures in January 2024 ordering Israel to take steps to prevent genocidal acts and enable humanitarian aid, among other specific measures — importantly, this was a provisional ruling on interim measures, not a final determination on the underlying genocide allegation itself, which remained pending before the Court as of 2026, a legal distinction this folio states precisely rather than characterising the case's ultimate outcome.
nodes.src: South Africa v. Israel, International Court of Justice, filed December 2023; provisional measures order, 26 January 2024; the case's final merits determination remained pending as of 2026.

nodes.label: The October 7 attack
nodes.full: The 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, whose treatment is centred in the Israeli folio.
